stances.claim: The CA's bypass of Duterte's ad-interim appointees to Comelec (chair Pangarungan; commissioners Garcia and Torrefranca-Neri), COA (chair Justol), CSC (chair Nograles), and 115 AFP officers is the operation of Article VII Section 16: ad-interim appointments are 'effective only until after disapproval by the [CA] or until the next adjournment of the Congress' -- so they automatically ended at midnight on June 4 when Congress adjourned (the CA adjourned June 1).

The CA is a 'political, not a judicial, body' -- composed of 12 senators and 12 representatives with the Senate president as ex-officio chair -- so its actions or inaction (here, the stated reason 'to give President-elect Ferdinand Bongbong Marcos Jr. a free hand in selecting his own officials') 'cannot be reviewed by the judiciary, except -- in my humble opinion -- for grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction.'

All official acts and opinions the bypassed officials rendered during their terms remain valid and legal. Their ad-interim appointments are 'deemed by law to be permanent, not temporary' -- meaning they could not have been removed by Duterte during the appointment, and if confirmed could have been removed only 'by the tedious process of impeachment.' Compensations and perks received are legal and valid; retirement benefits possible.
Their 'orphaned offices' may be filled by remaining commissioners on a temporary basis -- as the four remaining Comelec members did in electing Socorro Inting as acting Comelec chair.

Duterte cannot re-appoint them ad-interim because Article VII Section 15 bars presidential appointments 'two months immediately before the next presidential election and up to the end of his term, except temporary appointments to executive positions when continued vacancies therein will prejudice public service or endanger public safety' -- and the three independent commissions are NOT 'executive positions.' Moreover, Brilliantes v. Yorac (December 18, 1990) bars 'acting' appointments to the Comelec, with the same logic extending to COA and CSC.

Former commissioner Garcia's no-regrets disposition -- happily returning to non-partisan election-law practice and teaching after a few months of service, having served as counsel for BBM in his protest vs Robredo and for Sen. Migz Zubiri vs Koko Pimentel -- models the right ethical posture toward bypassed service.

Incoming Senate president Sen. Migz Zubiri deserves congratulation as 'a consensus builder, an honest public servant, and a gentleman of the old school' -- vindicated by his August 3, 2011 voluntary resignation 'without admitting any fault and with [his] vehement denial of the alleged electoral fraud,' which paved the way for Koko Pimentel and was rewarded by electoral wins in 2016 and 2022.
stances.rhetorical_move: named-exemplar of high ethical conduct rewarded

notable_anecdotes: CA's stated reason for bypassing the appointments -- 'to give President-elect Ferdinand Bongbong Marcos Jr. a free hand in selecting his own officials' -- preserved verbatim as the institutional rationale.
Comelec's institutional response: the four remaining members electing Commissioner Socorro Inting as acting chair -- modeling how independent commissions handle orphaned-office succession internally.

Garcia's no-regrets posture: 'no regrets in serving even for a few months only and would be happy to return to his practice and teaching of law' -- paired with the detail that he had been counsel for BBM in the Bongbong-Leni protest and for Migz Zubiri vs Koko Pimentel, modeling the non-partisan-expert ideal.

Zubiri's August 3, 2011 resignation -- 'without admitting any fault and with [his] vehement denial of the alleged electoral fraud hurled against (him)' -- preserved as the ethical-vindication backstory for his 2016 and 2022 electoral comebacks and now-impending Senate presidency.

one_paragraph_summary: After the Commission on Appointments bypassed President Duterte's ad-interim appointments to the leadership of the three constitutional commissions -- Comelec (chair Saidamen Pangarungan, commissioners George Garcia and Aimee Torrefranca-Neri), COA (chair Rizalina Justol), CSC (chair Karlo Nograles) -- and 115 AFP officers, with the stated reason 'to give President-elect Ferdinand Bongbong Marcos Jr. a free hand in selecting his own officials,' Panganiban explains the constitutional mechanics and their consequences. Article IX places the three independent commissions under 7-year terms 'without reappointment'; vacancies in their leadership arose from February 2 onward, prompting Duterte's recess ad-interim appointments. Under Article VII Section 16, ad-interim appointments are 'effective only until after disapproval by the [CA] or until the next adjournment of the Congress' -- so all the appointments automatically ended at midnight on June 4 when Congress adjourned (the CA adjourned June 1). The CA is 'a political, not a judicial, body' of 12 senators and 12 representatives with the Senate president as ex-officio chair; its decisions cannot be judicially reviewed except -- 'in my humble opinion' -- 'for grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction.' Importantly, all official acts and opinions rendered during the ad-interim terms remain valid and legal; the appointments themselves are 'deemed by law to be permanent, not temporary' (so they could not have been removed by Duterte during the term, and would have been removable only by impeachment if confirmed); compensations and perks received are legal; retirement benefits possible. The 'orphaned offices' may be filled by remaining commissioners temporarily -- as the four remaining Comelec members did by electing Commissioner Socorro Inting as acting Comelec chair. Duterte cannot re-appoint them ad-interim because Article VII Section 15 bars appointments 'two months immediately before the next presidential election and up to the end of his term, except temporary appointments to executive positions when continued vacancies therein will prejudice public service or endanger public safety' -- and the three independent commissions are NOT 'executive positions.' Brilliantes v. Yorac (December 18, 1990) independently bars 'acting' appointments to the Comelec, with the same reasoning applying to COA and CSC. CJ closes with two appreciations: former commissioner George Garcia's no-regrets disposition -- happily returning to non-partisan election-law practice and teaching (he had been counsel for BBM in his protest vs Robredo and for Sen. Migz Zubiri vs Koko Pimentel) -- and a congratulation to incoming Senate president Sen. Juan Miguel 'Migz' Zubiri as 'a consensus builder, an honest public servant, and a gentleman of the old school,' vindicated by his August 3, 2011 voluntary resignation 'without admitting any fault and with [his] vehement denial of the alleged electoral fraud hurled against (him),' which paved the way for Koko Pimentel and was rewarded by his electoral wins in 2016 and 2022.
